newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai government vows to boost slow economy.
newsitem.headline: New Thai government vows to boost slow economy.

text.p: Thailand's new government on Wednesday detailed major policy initiatives to tackle the slowing national economy.

In a policy statement to be presented to parliament later in the day and obtained by Reuters, the government identified the wide current account deficit as a key problem that needed to be curbed by boosting revenues and reducing spending.

The statement said another major plank in its economic policy would be the upholding of financial discipline to stabilise the slowing national economy, hit by sluggish exports growth and slow investment.
The government also said that it would deregulate the Thai financial sector in stages, but did not give a time frame for the process to yield results.
It aimed to boost Thailand's competitives in the region by further developing its money and capital markets, the statement added.
Focus on the slowing economy has been a key issue for Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, whose coalition government came to power earlier this month after elections in mid-November.
The economy, which experienced nearly nine percent growth for a decade until 1995, is expected by private economists to slow to just over six percent this year.

The central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said last week he expected the current account deficit to widen by up to 8.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year. In 1995, the gap was 8.1 percent of GDP.
Latest Bank of Thailand data also showed that Thai exports growth was 0.9 percent in the first nine months of this year compared with 20 percent growth posted in the same period in 1995.

The slowing Thai economy and recent political instability, ahead of the November 17 polls, also took its toll on the Thai stock market as foreign investors were sidelined and pushed the bourse now to near three-year-lows.
At 0325 GMT, the Thai SET index was up 4.13 points to 893.59.
To narrow the wide current account gap, the government said it would also seek to increase public, private and household savings and cut dependence on foreign borrowings.
"(The government) will boost revenue and cut unnecessary spending and ineffective investment," the statement said.

Thailand's short-term debt has been a cause of concern for the central bank and foreign investors. Central bank data showed that short-term foreign debt rose to $41.1 billion at end-1995 from $15.4 billion at end-1991.
Every new Thai government is required by the constitution to present its policy to the parliament before starting to administer the country.
The opposition plans to attack the planned new initiatives and said that while these sounded impressive they lacked details and time frames for yielding results.
They added that the new government had also failed to address key issues like corruption and illegal businesses which discouraged foreign investors from coming to Thailand.
